title: Dissolve Jump Cut in every Martin Scorsese Film

commenti.body: You’ll have to ask his longtime editor Thelma Schoonmaker for her reasoning. If you can understand the rules of editing and storytelling through editing, you can more easily break them, or use them for more creative types of cuts. It’s super effective!

She seems to follow more of a flow than strictly adhering to the "rules." I'd have to watch these specific scenes to see how they function. Mainly because I'm curious.

Some editors are highly regimented and have a particular workflow in how they break down scenes, and others just go with whatever works best to convey the chatachter and mood. Sometimes, you just need to do some other shit based on what was captured. Interesting thought about the juxtaposition between fast time and slow time. Maybe that's exactly why he does it, for that juxtaposition. Turn something mundane like getting out of the car into something just a little strange and disorienting. Similar to the vertigo shot (using zoom and camera movement while maintaining the subject's framing) which he uses a lot.

i'm an editor. i love doing a dissolve jump cut. it is a bit retro, but if you nail it, it can feel seamless, accelerating through a shot for which there is no superior cutaway, without notably increasing the pace. it can give action a dreamy feel, or a fun feel, depending on what's being depicted.

i usually dig her jazz-like editorial approach. i think scorsese obviously empowers it, too. but killers of the flower moon was her weakest edited works in a while. i think she may need to retire—in which case, scorsese may too.

OP is talking about the dissolve itself, which is not dissolving between scenes but rather just dissolving to a later point in the same shot. As you say, it may just be for pace, but it is kind of jarring, especially since the camera isn't locked, so even if you're not looking at the car, the text on the signs gets weirdly blurry during the dissolve as well.

I also noticed that he's weirdly approaching from the wrong side of the car. If he's leaving from the driver's side door, he should already be to the left of the car after getting out. But instead, he's walking across the front of the car from the right. Makes me think that some story beat was cut out of the middle of a oner, so they had to stitch the halves together. Him checking the wrong building or something like that.

It's a way to remove something unwanted from the shot. A lens flare, but probably just unwanted time -- that extra second or two. Similarly, one might think I have several hundred characters worth of thoughts about this matter, but I'm only trying to impress the bot who removes short posts.

Here, thanks to the person commented.

We don’t see him getting out of the car, he straight out of it after a cut, the jump cut (Jump in time)

But the cut is blurry, which is called a dissolve.

Two very different cuts, since they’re together, I named it a “dissolve jump cut”.

This technique can be seen as far back as Shane. I think I might have even seen this in a Kurosawa film. As others have mentioned, it is just a way to quicken the pace of an action. A hard jump cut has a feeling of urgency whereas the dissolve doesn’t affect the pace or rhythm in such a jarring manner.

The scene I’m referring to in Shane is a good example. Wilson walks in the bar and as he slowly walks in it dissolves to him walking further into the room. A jump cut would negatively impact the feel and pacing of the scene. The dissolve maintains the pace even though the action is condensed.
